title: Provider escape-hatch playbook: automated fallback & procurement triggers for inference outages
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Objective:
Create a practical, testable playbook that product, infra, and platform teams can use to detect model/provider degradation (latency/quality/cost) and execute automated or manual escape-hatch actions (routing, reduced feature set, procurement triggers). The doc should bridge competitive intelligence, market research on alternative model suppliers, and operational runbooks so that enterprise customers retain predictable UX during supply shocks.

Background & problem statement:
Redwood customers depend on low-latency, predictable inference. When a primary hosted model or third-party provider degrades or becomes unavailable (regional outage, supply shortage, model deprecation or licensing change), customers face service regressions or unexpected cost increases. We need a codified flow that ties signals (latency, error rate, quality eval drift, cost-per-token) to deterministic actions (route to alternate model, switch to dedicated capacity, enable quantized fallback, throttle nonessential routes, and trigger procurement).

Scope & non-goals:
- Scope: Product-facing playbook for 1) signal detection, 2) prioritized fallback strategies, 3) procurement/contract escalation triggers, 4) comms guidance for affected customers, 5) monitoring and post-incident retrospective. Includes signal thresholds and decision matrices.
- Non-goal: Implementation-level orchestration code (ENG will own infra automation tasks). Not a legal contract negotiation template.

Hypotheses to validate:
1) A small set of orthogonal signals (99th percentile latency over 3m, quality regression on key prompt set, sustained cost/unit delta > 30%) will correctly identify true provider incidents vs noise with <10% false positive rate.
2) Having two prioritized fallback model variants (low-latency quantized + mixed-precision standard) reduces customer-visible errors by 85% in simulated outages.

Methodology & deliverables:
- Competitive & market scan: inventory 10 alternative model providers (open models + cloud vendors) with quantization support, latency benchmarks by region, cost tables, and operational SLAs. Deliverable: model-supply-thermometer spreadsheet and summary slide.
- Decision matrix: map signal combinations to actions (immediate route change, degrade features, notify sales/CS, trigger procurement). Deliverable: one-page decision matrix.
- Runbook & alerts: canonical PagerDuty playbook steps and automated policy definitions (ex: route to fallback if p99 latency > 600ms for 5m AND production eval-quality drop > 6%). Deliverable: runbook doc and alert rules.
- Simulated drills: two tabletop exercises + one canary outage test (non-prod) to validate end-to-end. Deliverable: drill notes and success criteria.

Success metrics:
- Mean time to safe fallback (MTTFallback) <= 3 minutes after threshold crossing in tests.
- Customer-visible errors reduced by >=80% in simulated outages.
- Playbook adoption: Ops + two enterprise CS teams trained and sign off.

Acceptance criteria:
- Playbook doc reviewed and approved by Product, Infra, Security, and Legal (where applicable).
- Automated alert rules created in monitoring with annotated thresholds.
- Two fallback model vendors qualified and runbook steps validated in canary.

Risks & trade-offs:
- Cost: routing to dedicated capacity or expensive providers increases unit cost; playbook should include cost-to-availability guidance and payment triggers.
- Quality: fallback models may produce degraded semantics; prioritize graceful degradation (e.g., reduce response verbosity or revert to cached responses) over silent quality regressions.
- SLAs & contracts: procurement triggers can be slow; include temporary mitigations (regional routing, cached responses) while procurement runs.
